notes: Burns/Barke procedure appeal; Dyson LJ's analysis of EAT jurisdiction and case management is authoritative and detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Barke v Seetec: lawfulness of the Burns EAT reasons procedure

statutes_considered.title: Employment Tribunals (Constitution and Rules of Procedure) Regulations 2004

key_facts: Mrs Barke appealed disability discrimination and unfair dismissal decisions of an employment tribunal whose written reasons ran to 81 paragraphs.
Burton J, President of the EAT, invited the employment tribunal to answer specified questions under the Burns procedure before determining the appeal.
The appeal challenged whether the EAT had jurisdiction to request clarification or supplementation of tribunal reasons rather than remitting after allowing the appeal.
The DTI intervened supporting the Employment Tribunals Service view that the Burns procedure was an important case-management tool.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on the lawfulness of the Burns procedure inviting further written reasons from the employment tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Burns procedure is a lawful exercise of the EAT's powers and was appropriately used in this case.
enrichment.ratio: The EAT may lawfully invite an employment tribunal to clarify, supplement or give written reasons where reasons are missing or inadequate before finally disposing of an appeal; this differs from post-appeal remission, saves cost and delay, and is supported by section 35 and rule 30 of the 2004 regulations together with the overriding objective.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT has jurisdiction to request further reasons under the Burns procedure
Whether an employment tribunal is functus officio once judgment and reasons are entered on the register
Whether the Ermakov approach to supplementary reasons in judicial review should govern the Burns procedure
Whether the order made in Mrs Barke's case was an appropriate exercise of the jurisdiction

notes: Tree Preservation Order case stated; Rose and Crane LJJ's answers on group protection and age findings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: JR Charles v Barnet: Tree Preservation Order convictions upheld
key_facts: JR Charles & Son Ltd was convicted of lopping and wilfully destroying Cypress trees in Group 10 of a 1973 Tree Preservation Order at Pine Grove, Totteridge.
The company argued the protected group referred only to Lawson Cypress whereas the trees were Leyland Cypress and that no precise age finding had been made.
Magistrates found T1 and T2 were part of protected Group G10 on 28 May 2003 though they made no finding as to precise age.
The case stated was amended after an application to Hughes J, with costs reserved for the final outcome.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Barnet magistrates' convictions for contravening a Tree Preservation Order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions upheld and questions answered in favour of the council, with the appellant ordered to pay the respondent's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates may convict for breach of a group Tree Preservation Order without stating the precise age of the trees provided they find the particular trees were in existence and covered by the order when made; species evidence is relevant evidentially to identify protected trees rather than as a separate legal precondition.
legal_issues: Whether the type of Cypress tree was crucial to protection under the order
Whether convictions could stand without a finding of the precise age of T1 and T2
Whether T1 and T2 formed part of the protected group G10
Whether Article 2 of the order resolved ambiguity between the schedule and map

confidence.notes: Answers to the stated questions and dismissal of the appeal are explicit though some evidential findings in the case stated were sparse.

notes: CPA/CSCI star-rating appeal; Court of Appeal's reasoning on section 99 and independent judgment is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Audit Commission v Ealing: unlawful automatic CPA downgrade from CSCI rating
key_facts: Ealing challenged its Comprehensive Performance Assessment categorisation as 'weak' after the Audit Commission automatically downgraded the council because CSCI gave social services a zero-star rating.
Walker J held the Audit Commission acted unlawfully by adopting a rule that subordinated its own findings to CSCI's star rating without applying its own mind.
The Audit Commission appealed, arguing it could routinely adopt specialist bodies' findings where authorities made no representations.
Ealing's holistic CPA assessment had otherwise categorised the council as 'good' before the social care override.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review of the Audit Commission's CPA categorisation of Ealing London Borough Council.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the automatic downgrade rule was unlawful though the Commission may adopt specialist findings in most cases where they are not determinative.
enrichment.ratio: Section 99 requires the Audit Commission itself to make findings and categorisations; it may not adopt a rigid rule automatically downgrading an authority because another body gave a zero-star rating without considering whether that rating warrants downgrading, though in non-determinative cases specialist conclusions may be adopted after brief representations.
legal_issues: Construction of section 99 of the Local Government Act 2003
Whether the Audit Commission unlawfully subordinated its CPA findings to CSCI
Extent to which specialist body ratings may be adopted in CPA assessments
Whether a determinative zero-star social care rating must be independently evaluated
linked_authorities: Lavender v Minister of Housing and Local Government [1970] 1 WLR 1231

notes: Adverse possession/compulsory acquisition trial; Rimer J's analysis of vesting and limitation is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Hill v Transport for London: adverse possession and compulsory vesting
key_facts: Norman Hill and Terence Welford claimed title to land under ten arches supporting the A13 flyover at Canning Town by adverse possession.
Transport for London disputed the claim after the land vested in TfL on 3 July 2000 following compulsory acquisition from the Crown.
The claimants contended their prior adverse possession extinguished TfL's title at the moment of vesting, entitling them to compensation.
The dispute concerned airspace and land between the arches rather than the structure itself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Chancery Division on whether claimants had acquired title by adverse possession against TfL after compulsory vesting.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants' adverse possession claim failed; TfL retained title and no compensation was payable on the facts found.
enrichment.ratio: Where property is compulsorily acquired and vests in a new owner, the critical question is whether the claimant had already extinguished the transferor's title by adverse possession before vesting; possession after vesting runs against the new owner and does not retrospectively defeat the acquisition.
legal_issues: Whether adverse possession extinguished title at the moment of vesting in TfL
Whether the claimants had dispossessed the Crown before 3 July 2000
Application of limitation principles to land compulsorily acquired
Whether the claim was in reality a compensation claim rather than possession

confidence.notes: Facts, legal framing and outcome on vesting are clearly stated though detailed limitation reasoning is case-specific.

notes: TCC strike-out application; Jackson J's refusal to strike untidy particulars is concise and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Atos Consulting v Avis: strike-out for obstructive pleadings refused
key_facts: Atos Consulting sued Avis Europe in the Technology and Construction Court over a consultancy dispute.
Avis applied to strike out the particulars of claim as likely to obstruct the just disposal of proceedings because they were untidy and repleaded in the reply.
Avis did not pursue the abuse of process limb and concentrated on CPR 3.4(2)(b).
Jackson J found no authority for striking out on these grounds alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to strike out particulars of claim in TCC proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Strike-out application dismissed; the court had no jurisdiction or, alternatively, it would be wrong to strike out on the grounds advanced.
enrichment.ratio: The court should not strike out a statement of case merely because pleadings are untidy or partially repleaded in a reply where no abuse of process is shown; case management under the overriding objective does not permit the court to dictate how a party should plead its case.
legal_issues: Whether untidy particulars likely to obstruct just disposal justify strike-out under CPR 3.4(2)(b)
Whether repleading issues in the reply is an abuse warranting strike-out
Limits of court intervention in pleading under the overriding objective
Jurisdiction to strike out for procedural infelicities alone

confidence.notes: Short interlocutory judgment with explicit refusal and clear reasoning on principle.

notes: Post-SDT appeal costs judgment; divisional court's interim payment order is brief and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Simms v Law Society: interim costs payment after struck-off appeal
key_facts: Paul Francis Simms appealed unsuccessfully to the divisional court against a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal decision striking him off for dishonesty and related breaches.
The Law Society sought an interim payment on account of its costs of the appeal and of the SDT proceedings.
Simms appeared in person; the Law Society was represented by leading counsel.
The court had dismissed the substantive appeal in an earlier judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judgment on costs following dismissal of appeal from the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Interim costs order made for £80,000 on account of appeal costs only; no interim order made in respect of SDT costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a successful respondent in disciplinary appeal proceedings establishes a clear case for an interim payment, the court may order a sum reflecting the minimum likely to be awarded on detailed assessment of appeal costs, but need not extend that order to earlier tribunal costs.
legal_issues: Whether an interim payment on account of costs was appropriate
Whether interim payment should include SDT costs as well as appeal costs
Quantum of interim payment reflecting minimum likely assessment
Costs consequences after dismissal of solicitor's appeal
linked_authorities: Simms v The Law Society [2005] EWHC 408 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Short costs judgment with explicit quantum and scope of the interim order.

notes: Homelessness policy challenge; Wilkie J's declarations on section 193 and joint tenancies are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Hammia v Wandsworth: unlawful homelessness duty precondition
key_facts: Mr Hammia's partner Miss Malika fled domestic violence from their joint Wandsworth secure tenancy at Whitgate House.
Wandsworth accepted a section 193 duty only if she relinquished the joint tenancy by serving a notice to quit, pursuant to an allocation scheme policy.
Miss Malika signed a notice to quit in October 2003 and the council then discharged its duty; possession proceedings followed against Mr Hammia.
The claimant challenged the policy and decision letter of 30 September 2003 by judicial review while county court possession proceedings were adjourned.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Wandsworth's homelessness policy and decision letter requiring joint tenants to quit before accepting a Part 7 duty.
enrichment.outcome: Policy declaration granted that requiring joint secure tenants fleeing violence to terminate their tenancy before accepting a section 193 duty is unlawful; declaration on the notice to quit refused; defendant ordered to pay 70% of costs.
enrichment.ratio: Once a local authority is satisfied that the section 193 criteria are met the main housing duty arises and it is unlawful to impose an additional requirement that a homeless joint tenant relinquish an existing secure tenancy before accepting the duty, though a similar requirement may be lawful at the stage of discharging the duty under section 206.
legal_issues: Whether Wandsworth unlawfully imposed extra-statutory conditions before accepting a section 193 duty
Whether the allocation scheme policy applied to homeless applicants with existing tenancies
Whether the September 2003 decision letter manifested an unlawful policy
Whether the notice to quit was invalid and unenforceable

confidence.notes: Policy declaration, distinction from section 206 discharge, and partial success on remedies are clearly reasoned.

notes: POCA civil recovery appeal; Court of Appeal's section 308(9) analysis on quashed confiscation orders is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Assets Recovery Agency v Singh: civil recovery after quashed confiscation
key_facts: Satnam Singh was convicted in 1998 of excise fraud and a confiscation order of £300,000 was made in 1999.
The confiscation order was quashed in December 2002 because of procedural defects in the confiscation proceedings.
The Assets Recovery Agency sought civil recovery under POCA 2002 and obtained an interim receiving order over Singh's assets.
Singh argued section 308(9) barred recovery because his benefit had already been taken into account in the original confiscation order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal concerning whether civil recovery under POCA was barred after an earlier confiscation order had been quashed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in the Agency's favour; a quashed confiscation order is treated as never having been made so section 308(9) did not prevent civil recovery.
enrichment.ratio: Property is not excluded from civil recovery under section 308(9) where a confiscation order taking account of the defendant's benefit has been quashed; the quashed order is null and void and the statutory bar against double recovery does not apply to assets never validly recovered.
legal_issues: Construction of section 308(9) of POCA 2002
Effect of a quashed confiscation order on later civil recovery
Whether property had been taken into account for confiscation purposes
Lawfulness of interim receiving orders pending civil recovery
linked_authorities: Assets Recovery Agency v Singh [2004] EWHC 2335 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Central statutory issue and treatment of quashed confiscation orders are clearly resolved though some procedural history is complex.

notes: Conservatory negligence appeal; Court of Appeal's breach and contributory negligence analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: James v Butler: conservatory rafter negligence and contributory negligence
key_facts: Raymond James was struck in the eye by a falling conservatory rafter while bringing coffee to Alan Butler, who was erecting the structure for £300.
Butler had finger-tightened a securing screw and left the rafter temporarily unsupported while fetching a screwdriver.
The recorder held Butler had not been negligent because a general labourer could reasonably think the rafter was safe and found 50% contributory negligence.
Damages of about £44,525 were agreed if liability was established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Taunton County Court judgment dismissing a personal injury claim for inadequate securing of a roof rafter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; full damages of £44,525.32 awarded with no contributory negligence; appellant to have 50% of costs below and costs in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant undertaking paid building work owes at least the care of a reasonably skilled DIY enthusiast; finger tightening a securing screw without ensuring it has engaged is breach of duty where the rafter then falls without external force, and a claimant entering the conservatory in those circumstances is not contributorily negligent.
legal_issues: Standard of care owed by a general building labourer erecting a conservatory
Whether mistaken belief that a rafter was secure excused breach of duty
Whether the claimant was contributorily negligent in entering the conservatory
Whether the case should be remitted for rehearing on liability

confidence.notes: Liability reasoning, rejection of contributory negligence and final order are explicit.

notes: Robbery sentence appeal; Hughes LJ's reduction for duress-related subsidiary offending is clear.

enrichment.short_title: R v Chirnside: robbery sentence reduced for duress circumstances
key_facts: Paul William Chirnside, a soldier, robbed security guards delivering £20,000 to a North Tyneside supermarket using a machete in June 2004.
He pleaded guilty on the basis he acted under duress from a drug creditor though he had voluntarily exposed himself to that risk.
He was on leave, heavily using alcohol and cocaine, and the money was never recovered.
Newcastle Crown Court sentenced him to six years' imprisonment in November 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence for robbery with a machete.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentence reduced from six years to four and a half years.
enrichment.ratio: Where robbery is committed by a subsidiary offender recruited and operating under threat, albeit after voluntarily exposing himself to the risk through drug-related indebtedness, a sentence below the ordinary range may be justified when the Crown and judge accept the factual basis of the plea.
legal_issues: Whether six years was manifestly excessive for machete robbery
Effect of a guilty plea basis involving duress and subsidiary participation
Relevance of the offender's military service and drug addiction
Appropriate reduction for unusual coercive circumstances

confidence.notes: Facts, accepted plea basis and reduced sentence are clearly recorded though detailed sentencing guidelines discussion is limited.
